item.title: SC makes protection from arrest ‘absolute’ for journalist who reported on Ayodhya theft allegations
item.description: The bench said the police’s request for three months’ worth of social media data predating the alleged road rage incident ‘seems to be an overkill’.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday made absolute the interim protection from coercive action granted to journalist Abhishek Upadhyay in a road rage case and any subsequent first information reports, The Hindu reported.

The bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi also quashed a notice issued by the Uttar Pradesh Police to social media platform X that sought data pertaining to Upadhyay’s account, Live Law reported. The notice had sought data covering a three-month period before the alleged road rage incident.

Upadhyay has claimed that the road rage case was filed to harass him for his reports on the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple in Ayodhya. He was among the first to report on the alleged corruption.

In a petition against the first information report against him, Upadhyay had filed an application challenging the police’s notice to X.

During a hearing on September 7, the counsel for Upadhyay stated that the police’s notice had sought information about the account dating back to June 1, even though the FIR in the road rage case had been filed on August 18.

The lawyer argued that the police were trying to identify Upadhyay’s journalistic sources.

item.title: Modi’s bigger challenge: What people away from protest sites are saying about his government
item.description: The protests have blown the lid off a growing number of grievances: SIR, inflation, farm distress, education inequality, rising health costs.
item.content:encoded:
A surly-looking elderly man sat behind the counter of an empty jewellery store in Delhi’s bustling Karol Bagh on October 11, reading The Sunday Times of India.

“Restrained, detained, contained,” said the front page banner headline of the newspaper, describing the events of the previous day.

The jeweller grumbled and put it more pithily: “Such a nuisance.”

On Saturday, thousands of ordinary citizens had defied the unprecedented security cover in Central Delhi to show up to protest against the chief election commissioner who they believe is rigging voter lists in the ruling party’s favour.

To thwart the protest, the government had cancelled trains, closed down metro stations, and even shuttered markets like Karol Bagh.

The jeweller, who did want to disclose his name, said he was feeling “very frustrated” – it was the start of the festive season, and chaos on the streets was not good for business. “There has been a lot of disturbance and it is not going to be over soon,” he said.

His annoyance with the protestors aside, he was sympathetic to their cause. “There is definitely something fishy about the voting system currently,” he said.

item.title: Becoming Agarwal: A new book examines how a dominant mercantile caste sustains its privilege today
item.description: An excerpt from the Introduction to ‘Becoming Agarwal: The Manufacture of a Close-Knit Mercantile Caste’, by Ujithra Ponniah.
item.content:encoded:
The “new” Hindu India is an elite, exclusionary and violent project characterised by an ethnic democracy led by members of wealthy “upper”-caste Hindu groups and increasingly finding cultural resonance across caste groups. An ethnic democracy is one in which there is a two-tiered citizenship, with the majority having more rights than the minority. The BJP is traditionally seen as the Brahmin-Bania party. The majority rise of the BJP in 2014 and again for a second term in 2019 has seen an increase in the structural power of business.

In 2009, [Christophe] Jaffrelot and [Narender] Kumar wrote about the “plebeianisation” – or the rise of the lower castes in political power – by showing how the share of upper-caste members of legislative assemblies (MLAs) has steadily declined in many states from the 1950s to the 2000s. Two decades later, this trend was reversed, and Jaffrelot and [Giles] Vernier argued that there was a resurgence of political elites from upper castes in the Hindu belt along with non-dominant OBCs through the BJP’s careful social engineering. This came at the expense of sliding representation of women and religious minorities.

The protest began after Bharatiya Janata Party leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam was named as the next governor of Sikkim on Monday.

Bhandari’s family and activists have alleged that Gautam is the alleged VIP linked to the murder case. They were demanding that the BJP leader not be allowed to assume his new post until the allegations against him are investigated.

The parents were released less than two hours after they were detained, ANI reported.

They were detained hours after Opposition leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, along with several Congress MPs, had joined the protest on Wednesday. The Congress leaders and party workers had remained at the site after Gandhi and Vadra left.

item.title: The pure feast of colour that is Kamal Amrohi’s ‘Pakeezah’
item.description: The interweave of emotion and colour stands out in a restoration carried out by Film Heritage Foundation along with Kamal Amrohi’s family.
item.content:encoded:
In Kamal Amrohi’s Pakeezah, there are early references to colour and the psychological states it evokes.

The courtesan Nargis tells her aristocratic lover Shahabuddin who has promised to marry her that she can already imagine the house they will be living in. The house will be white, like their pure love. Nargis dreams of crossing the threshold dressed in bridal red threads.

As the story unfolds, viewers learn that Nargis’s profession comes in the way of the marriage, leading to her early death. Shahabuddin switches to black sherwanis, the shade of mourning as he hunts for Sahebjaan, the daughter he has had with Nargis.

Sahebjaan is the leading light of Delhi’s pleasure quarter. Bedecked out in an array of bright ensembles (flame orange, coral pink, emerald green), Sahebjaan entices her patrons even as she longs to be known as “pakeezah”, the symbol of purity and respectability. Away from the dance floor, Sahebjaan is seen mostly in white, the colour-coded expression of her yearning.

Pakeezah, as cinephiles know, is a classic among Indian colour films. But not so many remember that it was initially shot in black and white. Made over a 15-year period and finally released in 1972, Pakeezah was interrupted by Amrohi’s decision to reshoot in colour and...

item.title: ‘SC will not do anything’: Why lawyers are disillusioned by court silence on Delhi police excesses
item.description: Lawyers pointed out that the Supreme Court has not passed any significant order against the Delhi Police and Centre despite multiple petitions.
item.content:encoded:
On October 10, Anna Oommen, a 28-year-old advocate in the Supreme Court, stood on a road outside the Supreme Court with dozens of lawyers, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

As they marched towards Mandi House, past heavy barricades, they were halted by the police near a gate of the Supreme Court. “By the third barricade, my hair was being pulled by a woman police officer,” Oommen told Scroll. “They pulled my neck and collar, my kurti was pulled. I was pushed with such force that I experienced difficulty in breathing and was left gasping for air for several minutes.”

Anne Mathew, another advocate who was part of the protest, saw Oommen struggle to breathe and ran to help her. But four to five female police personnel pushed both into a bus. “We were physically lifted, pushed and dragged into the bus,” Mathew said. “Anna was dealt with especially roughly.”

For about 30 minutes, they were confined in the stationary bus, with its windows shut. When the bus finally started moving, they were not told about where they were taken. Their requests for drinking water were denied.

item.title: Pakistan and Turkey will send help to Saudi Arabia but are unlikely to fight Houthi rebels
item.description: Under the Mecca pact, Islamabad has committed only to the defence of holy cities in the Gulf country while Turkey has yet to ratify the agreement.
item.content:encoded:
Within two months of it being signed, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan invoked the Mecca mutual defence pact in response to attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebel forces.

The three countries agreed on October 5 to activate what Saudi defence minister Khalid bin Salman called collective deterrence measures against the Houthis. Islamabad and Ankara have undertaken to provide “agreed military forces and capabilities” and ensure their rapid deployment to the kingdom.

The same day this agreement was struck, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces opened a counteroffensive, supported by 100 Saudi-led coalition jets from Arab and regional states, to push the Houthis back from the Bab al-Mandab, the strait they seized in September.

For a month it had looked as if the pact may turn out to be a hollow promise. Islamabad and Ankara issued messages of condemnation after a string of Houthi rebel attacks on the kingdom, but did little else. Analysts were talking of the alliance as a stress test for the alliance. And the question was whether Pakistan and Turkey would fail the test. item.title: Centre to sell 60.7% stake in IDBI Bank to Canadian firm for Rs 52,000 crore
item.description: The divestment would bring the ‘largest foreign direct investment so far’, said the Ministry of Finance.
item.content:encoded:
The Indian government and Life Insurance Corporation will sell 60.7% stake in IDBI Bank for Rs 52,878 crore to Canadian financial holding company Fairfax Financial Holdings Limited, said the Union Ministry of Finance on Wednesday.

The divestment would bring the “largest foreign direct investment in the financial sector of our economy so far”, added the ministry.

It said that IDBI Bank had “required repeated infusion of capital, initially provided by the Government of India” and later by Life Insurance Corporation.

In view of this, the Reserve Bank of India imposed several restrictions on the bank and the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved strategic restructuring of the financial institution.

“In compliance thereof, it was decided that an aggregate 60.72% of the equity stake in the IDBI Bank Limited be sold to a strategic buyer,” said the ministry. This would leave a shareholding of 15% with the Union government and 19% with Life Insurance Corporation.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘At Her Beck and Call’ by Flora Annie Steel in ‘The Raj in Ghostly Light: Supernatural Stories from British India’, edited by BC Dutt.

“What is your name?” I asked.

“Phooli-jân, Huzoor,” she answered, with a brilliant dazzling smile.

I sat looking at her, wondering if a more appropriate name could have been found for that figure among the anemones and celandines, the primulas, pansies, and pinks – the thousand-and-one blossoms which, glowing against their groundwork of forget-me-nots, formed a jewel-mosaic right to the foot of the snows above us. Flowerful life! Truly that was hers. She had a great bunch of scarlet rhododendron stuck behind her ear, matching the cloth cap perched jauntily on her head, and as she sat herding her buffaloes on the upland she had threaded chaplet on chaplet of oxeyed daisies, and hung them about her wherever they could be hung. The result was distinctly flowerful; her face also was distinctly pretty, distinctly clean for a Kashmiri girl’s. item.title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence of Sri Lankan worker over alleged blasphemous comment
item.description: Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was convicted in September for an allegedly derogatory comment he had made about Islam and Prophet Muhammad.

A Saudi court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan migrant worker who had been convicted of blasphemy in September for a Facebook comment, said Sri Lankan Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra on Wednesday.

Anojan Sivarasa, 27, had been sentenced to death by a Saudi appellate court for an allegedly derogatory comment he had made about Islam and Prophet Muhammad, reported BBC.

In June, video footage of a Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims was widely shared on social media. During the religious arguments that followed online, a user reportedly posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity. In response, Sivarasa made the allegedly insulting comments, which he reportedly deleted later. He had also posted a video apologising for his alleged comment.

A screenshot of his comment was sent to his employer and Saudi officials, leading to him getting arrested in July, reported BBC.

The case had spurred diplomatic efforts by Sri Lanka to seek clemency for Sivarasa.

On Wednesday, Hemachandra said that the Supreme Court of Saudi Arabia had set aside the judgement imposing the death penalty on Sivarasa on Tuesday.

Hasina, who has been in Delhi since the collapse of her government in August 2024 following massive student-led protests, said that it was “deeply unfortunate” if her presence was the reason behind Rahman skipping the summit. She added that “short-term political calculations are inherently counterproductive”.

“Relations between two countries cannot be determined by personal considerations or political sensitivities involving one individual,” she told PTI.

On September 10, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir had said that Dhaka would not send a government representative to the BRICS Summit as Rahman was “not invited” to the meeting.

However, Bangladesh had received two invitations from India. One from Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a bilateral visit, while the other for Rahman, in his capacity as chairperson of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation to attend the BRICS summit which was held on September 12 and 13.

item.title: Ramachandra Guha: 70 years ago, Ambedkar’s conversion to Buddhism struck a blow against caste system
item.description: However, he died a mere seven weeks later, leaving unwritten the books he had planned on making the religion ‘respectable to the masses of the country’.
item.content:encoded:
My favourite newspaper no longer exists. It was called the Bombay Chronicle, and it was founded in 1910 as a nationalist alternative to the British-owned and British-oriented Times of India. In the first half of the 20th century, Bombay was an incredibly exciting place to live and work in. It was British India’s commercial capital, and also the epicentre of the film industry, of nationalist politics, and of much else besides. The excitement and intensity of the times was vividly captured in the pages of the Bombay Chronicle. The newspaper had many fine reporters and two outstanding editors: BG Horniman, who was at the helm in its early years, and SA Brelvi, who edited it in the 1920s and 1930s.

When I thought of writing a column on BR Ambedkar’s conversion to Buddhism, it was to the old files of Bombay Chronicle that I turned. I knew the paper had covered Ambedkar’s activities ever since he entered public life, and it would be interesting to see what it said about the last major event of his career. Fortunately, the newspaper was still around to cover the event, although by this time Horniman and Brelvi were both dead.

item.title: What is the most serious threat we face today? This book argues it is accelerating climate change
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Life in the Time of Polycrisis’, by G Madhusoodanan.
item.content:encoded:
The severest manifestation of the global polycrisis is climate change. The Earth’s climate is regulated by an enormously complex melange of interrelated processes, forming part of the planetary ecological web. The web includes the sun, the atmosphere, the lithosphere, the hydrosphere, the cryosphere, and the biosphere. These are interrelated and interact through many natural cycles or biogeochemical cycles. Scientific understanding of the Earth’s climate system progressed significantly in the twentieth century. The pioneer of climate science, the late Wallace Broecker, warned in 1987 that interfering in natural systems not fully scientifically understood is like “playing Russian roulette which may result in unpleasant surprises”, because no one knows what lies in the active chamber of the gun.

Russian roulette players know the risky game they are playing. But humans hardly knew the consequences when they embarked on the path of modern fossil-fuel-powered economic growth.

However, at the beginning of 1980, when empirical evidence emerged about the impact on climate, the initial reaction of governments and corporations was denial, and the denial industry continues even today. We are now in a climate emergency which is set within the larger interconnected polycrisis.

The incident occurred in the Raghopur police station area when the passengers were travelling to a nearby village to attend a feast.

item.description: As Indian students are forced to view medieval history through a polarised lens, the country’s democratic fabric faces a deep philosophical crisis.
item.content:encoded:
The new social science textbook for Class 9 students released by the National Council of Educational Research and Training has removed chapters on European revolutions to prioritise medieval Indian history through the lens of “Resistance and Resilience” against successive foreign invasions.

The textbook. titled Understanding Society: India and Beyond (Part 2), argues that the Indian subcontinent faced successive phases of invasions driven by territorial expansion and religious motives. It details the brutality of the Mughal state against Sikh gurus, alongside regional uprisings such as the Jat Uprising of 1669 against heavy agrarian taxation and religious policies.

While these historical conflicts and state oppressions are matters of historical record that deserve rigorous study, framing the entire medieval past through a monolithic, black-and-white binary of Muslim invasion versus Hindu resistance flattens the complex, messy realities of history. It replaces nuanced historical analysis with a political narrative of perpetual civilisational grievance.

By reducing history to an unceasing clash of religious forces, such textbooks commit a grave erase the profound cultural osmosis that occurred simultaneously at the grassroots level. History is rarely just a process of state-on-state violence or imperial conquest. Just as political conflicts unfolded, the everyday medieval landscape witnessed deep-seated synthesis – the evolution of Sufi and Bhakti philosophies, shared...

item.title: A new book traces the evolution of India’s ambition to become a centre of geopolitical power
item.description: An excerpt from ‘India after Nonalignment: The Quest to Become a Pole in International Politics’, by Happymon Jacob.
item.content:encoded:
A dominant strain of Indian strategic thought is anchored in a sense of civilisational greatness, powered by a collective memory of colonial subjugation, racism and systemic exclusion. This narrative overlaps several political timelines. During the freedom struggle, it was about emerging from colonial rule as a great power. But for the Hindu nationalists, it was also about shedding the shame of all past invasions into India, particularly by Muslim Mughals, and about Hindu pride. During the Cold War, it was about economic and political discrimination and nuclear “apartheid”, among others. In the post-Cold War world, it was about non-interference, US sanctions and the ills of American unipolarity.

For much of its post-Independence history, Indian behaviour expressed a siege mindset, born of persistent strategic anxieties that left its leaders little room to effectively articulate the country’s rightful place in the world. This sense of vulnerability and insecurity was a constant in the Indian strategic imagination. The sense of anxiety in the Indian political culture was felt across party divides. However, since the turn of the millennium, the “postcolonial insignificance” and external‘disciplinary pressures’ that once constrained New Delhi have dramatically diminished. item.title: ‘The Loves of a Mogul Prince’: The forgotten film that first tapped into the Anarkali legend
item.description: The movie would have been the first adaptation of the famous Imtiaz Ali Taj play ‘Anarkali’.
item.content:encoded:
In Indian popular culture, Salim and Anarkali are firmly embedded as being among the greatest lovers of all time. While the historical veracity of their forbidden romance – or whether Anarkali existed at all – is disputed, there is no debate about the role played by cinema in immortalising the legend.

Several screen versions of the story, most of them drawing heavily from the famous Imtiaz Ali Taj play Anarkali, have captivated audiences for nearly a century now. There is Nandlal Jaswantlal’s Anarkali (1953), starring Pradeep Kumar and Bina Rai and featuring a fabulous soundtrack by C Ramchandra. There is K Asif’s all-time classic Mughal-e-Azam (1960), starring Prithviraj Kapoor, Dilip Kumar and Madhubala.

Before these films, there was the Imperial Film Company’s silent movie Anarkali in 1928, which made Sulochana an even bigger star, and its talkie remake in 1935. Were it not for the acumen of Imperial Film Company founder Ardeshir Irani, another film titled The Loves of A Mogul Prince would have been the first adaptation of the doomed romance.

item.title: Why relocating wild animals is rife with complications
item.description: The social dimensions of moving wildlife were considered much less consistently than biological ones
item.content:encoded:
Moving large animals around is a seductive idea in conservation. If there are plenty of animals in one place and too few in another, moving some between the two seems an obvious solution. Sometimes it is. But with animals as large, mobile and socially complicated as elephants and rhinos, the move itself can turn out to be the straightforward part.

This autumn, 12 rhinos are due to be moved from a well-established reserve in North West Province in South Africa to another protected area, in the Waterberg region, as part of efforts to establish and strengthen secure rhino populations. I am involved with the conservation work around the move, including research that will follow what happens after the rhinos arrive.

But there are lessons from past projects that we have to bear in mind. In 2022, 263 elephants were moved around 350km from Liwonde National Park in Malawi to another park in Malawi, Kasungu National Park. Decades of poaching had severely depleted Kasungu’s elephants, while successful protection in Liwonde had allowed its population to grow. With Malawi’s protected areas increasingly isolated from one another, moving elephants from a relatively dense population to a much larger park with relatively few elephants made good sense.

item.title: Why Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize for Literature: For her bold, inventive, breathtaking work
item.description: The distance between classical literature and contemporary life shrinks thoroughly and repeatedly across her work.
item.content:encoded:
Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. The 76-year-old Canadian poet, essayist, translator and classicist was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the news broke. The Swedish Academy praised her “bold and inventive” oeuvre for its “playful dialogue with the classical tradition”, through which she has fashioned “new forms for contemporary literature”.

In books like her 1998 verse novel Autobiography of Red (which has sold nearly 100,000 copies in the United States), Wrong Norma (2024), her recent poetry collection, and her 1986 debut Eros the Bittersweet – a book-length essay about the god of love – she challenges formal conventions and moves across literary genres.

Carson’s own account of what language can do offers a sense of the possibilities such invention opens up:

“words can squirt sideways, mute and mad; you think they are tools, or toys, or tame, and all at once they burn all your clothes off and you’re standing there singed and ridiculous in the glare of the lightning.'“

‘The easiest difficult poet’

Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson studied classics at the University of Toronto and went on to teach ancient Greek. Eros the Bittersweet grew out of her scholarly training.

item.title: The economy is made of people: Lessons from the Economics Nobel for India
item.description: Macroeconomic outcomes cannot be fully understood without examining the individual decisions that produce them.
item.content:encoded:
What does a central bank’s interest-rate decision mean to a household struggling with food prices, a small business deciding whether to expand or a company weighing a new investment? These may seem like very different questions. Yet they lie at the heart of a single economic problem: how do the decisions of households and businesses shape the wider economy and how can public policy influence those decisions?

This question sits at the centre of the work recognised by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Robert E Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their research helps explain why understanding an economy requires looking beyond aggregate indicators to the choices, expectations and constraints of the people and firms that make it function.

For India, this is more than a theoretical insight. The latest figures show retail inflation rising to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, while food inflation climbed to 7.74%. The burden is not evenly distributed: rural headline inflation reached 6.08%, compared with 4.88% in urban areas.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘1965: Holding The Line at Asal Uttar’, by Harash Vir Singh and Shiv Kunal Verma.

The Khemkaran Sector lay in the southwestern part of the Bari Doab, the tract of land between the Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej rivers. To the south and east stood the Beas and the Sutlej. To the north ran the Grand Trunk Road. To the west lay the Ichhogil Canal. The international border ran a short distance to the west of the canal before turning towards the northeast. The entire stretch of ground had a gentle fall from the northeast towards the southwest. Every nala, distributary, and surface drain followed this natural slope, and over time these channels shaped both cultivation and movement across the countryside.

There were three principal canals in this area, all aligned broadly from the northeast to the southwest. These were the Upper Bari Doab Canal, the Kasur Branch, and the Sobraon Branch. Beyond the Sobraon Branch lay the Beas and the Sutlej. Together, these water bodies not only irrigated the land but also canalized movement and created corridors between embankments where wheels and tracks could travel with relative ease. The final rolls also include more than 7.9 lakh newly added voters, The New Indian Express reported.

item.title: Why weight lost by restricting calories doesn’t often stay off

item.content:encoded:
In the last few years, there’s been a lot of interest in calorie-restricted diets for weight loss.

These can vary significantly, from intermittent fasting (where you restrict eating to a certain window of the day), alternate day fasting (where you consume limited or no calories on every other day) to the Fast 800 which promotes rapid weight loss by drastically reducing calories with the “Mediterranean diet”.

The basic idea might seem obvious: reduce how much you eat, and you’ll theoretically lose weight.

But are they healthy? And will you just put the weight back on if you stop?

What are calorie-restricted diets?

The amount of energy you need each day varies based on your age, sex, body composition, how physically active you are, and any background health considerations.

Calorie-restricted diets aim to reduce a person’s overall energy (calorie) intake. And in certain instances, when managed carefully by health-care teams, there is evidence for their benefits beyond weight loss, including as an intervention before surgery.

The general aim is to eat less than the body uses, causing the body to draw on its stored energy – fat. Over time, this imbalance, generally using more energy than you eat, can lead to weight loss.

item.title: Can smallpox return from 500-year-old virus fragments?
item.description: The variola virus material found in Chile consists only of damaged genetic fragments preserved for centuries.
item.content:encoded:
Smallpox is the only human infectious disease to have been eradicated worldwide. Researchers have now recovered fragments of ancient DNA belonging to variola virus, the virus that causes smallpox, from the naturally mummified remains of two Indigenous people buried in northern Chile.

For centuries, smallpox caused devastating epidemics. Its severe form, variola major, killed around 30% of those infected, although the rate varied between outbreaks and populations.

The first documented outbreak in the Americas occurred on the island of Hispaniola in 1518. During the 16th century, successive epidemics became a major contributor to the catastrophic loss of Indigenous life, amid the wider violence and disruption of European colonisation.

In 1967, the World Health Organization (WHO) launched an intensified eradication programme, combining vaccination with surveillance and containment. The last-known naturally acquired case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

Live variola virus is officially retained at two high-security WHO-designated laboratories for approved research. The material found in Chile consists only of damaged genetic fragments preserved for centuries.

item.title: Nobel economics prize awarded to Robert Hall, Michael Woodford for stabilisation models
item.description: Their models have ‘significantly improved our ability to implement’ effective economic stabilisation policy, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.
item.content:encoded:
The Nobel Prize in economics was on Monday awarded to American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for stabilisation models.

Hall and Woodford developed new macroeconomic models that have “significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said.

A stabilisation policy is a set of macroeconomic measures that governments and central banks take to stabilise the business cycle, maintain employment levels and keep inflation under control.

Fiscal and monetary policy measures based on these models “can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs”, the academy said.

Hall and Woodford were awarded the prize for “demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy”, it added.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” said the academy. “This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”

The two economists will equally share the prize amount of 12 million Swedish kronor, or Rs 11.4 crore.

The prize in economics was the last to be announced this year.

The trade unionist’s home doubles up as the local office of the All India Central Council of Trade Unions, which is affiliated to the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation. He staved off the police for the night by asking them to call the next morning. But at 7 am, five officers arrived at his doorstep to detain him.

“They did not tell me any reason nor gave me any kind of legal document,” Abhishek said. “They kept asking me how many people are coming for the protest at Jantar Mantar. They had a list of activists from other unions. They asked about their whereabouts.”

item.title: Economy check: India aims to achieve net zero emissions by 2070. Is this feasible?
item.description: An excerpt from ‘India’s Green Transition’ by Nirvikar Singh in ‘The Indian Economy: Navigating a Global Turning Point’.
item.content:encoded:
India’s per capita energy consumption is less than 40% of the world’s average, but its energy system relies heavily on coal for power generation, as well as for industrial production. Oil is most important for transport, and biomass is most important for residential heating and cooking. Excluding biomass, in 2019, India’s total primary energy supply (TPES) was 734 million tons of oil equivalent (Mtoe), with just over half of this being covered by domestic production. Total final consumption (TFC) was 410 Mtoe, with industry accounting for the largest share, 42%, followed by the residential sector and transport.

India’s pattern of electricity generation and energy use imply that policies to achieve net zero have to have two main foci. The first is greatly increasing the role of cleaner sources of electricity generation, and the second is electrification of industrial production. There are differences across the studies, in terms of modelling and assumptions, but they all emphasise cleaner electricity and electrification.

Currently, electricity accounts for just over a quarter of India’s TFC. Electricity generation capacity in July 2024 was 448 GW, of which 10.47% was hydropower, while 1.82% was nuclear power. Arguably, neither of these sources affords significant scope for growth in capacity. On the...

item.title: ‘Angh’: How a film from Nagaland hopes to crack the Oscars – without being India’s official pick
item.description: Director Theja Rio, producer Nancy Nisa Beso and sales agent Gaurav Dhingra tell Scroll about the journey of the award-winning film.
item.content:encoded:
India will be represented at the 2027 Oscars by Gondhal, a Marathi-language psychological thriller by first-time director Santosh Davakhar. But another Indian debutant director’s film will also make a bid for the Academy Award for Best International Film: Theja Rio’s Angh.

The Konyak-language drama recounts the challenges faced by the Konyak community in Nagaland by the spread of Christianity. Set in 1962, a year before Nagaland became a state of the Indian Union, Angh chronicles the titular village chief’s valiant efforts to preserve his way of life.

An American Baptist missionary has converted everyone else in the village, which the Angh regards as a gross betrayal. The Angh’s animistic beliefs and ritualistic headhunting are at odds with the missionary’s preaching – a stand-off that also causes tensions between the Angh and his son.

Although Angh is not India’s official entry to the Oscars, it is charting its own path, boosted by a major award at the Toronto International Film Festival in September. Angh won the top prize in the Platform section, a feat that automatically qualifies the Indian production for the international feature film Oscar.

item.title: As Harvard launches course with AI professors, what is the future of teaching in India?
item.description: Technology could help fill the gaps in the country’s education infrastructure but perhaps teachers are not so easy to replace – yet.
item.content:encoded:
An eight-week online entrepreneurship bootcamp launched by Harvard Business School lets participants pitch a start-up idea to an artificial-intelligence avatar modelled on a real professor.

The HBS Foundry programme, designed to train aspiring entrepreneurs, costs $699, or roughly Rs 67,000. Participants are taken through the entire process of building a start-up, from refining an idea to pitching it to investors and customers.

The programme combines course material from Harvard Business School, AI agents trained on faculty expertise, a community of fellow entrepreneurs and simulated video conversations with AI avatars. The plan is to take Harvard’s entrepreneurship training to far more than the roughly 900 students the business school admits each year – and there are many takers, according to The New York Times.

The HBS Foundry programme raises questions about the future of higher education and the role of teachers. item.title: Infections are causing cancer, finds new research
item.description: Just five pathogens, including HPV, were found to be the main causes.
item.content:encoded:
Around 12% of the world’s total cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organization.

The study, published today in The Lancet Oncology, analysed the frequency and causes of different cancers, specifically examining the role of infections.

It linked 2.3 million new cancer cases to an infection. Most were caused by just five pathogens: Helicobacter pylori (4%), human papillomavirus, or HPV (4%), hepatitis B (2%), Epstein-Barr virus (1%) and hepatitis C (under 1%). These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers.

So, how can an infection cause cancer? And does this mean these cancers are preventable?

Did we already know about this link?

Some of the study authors have been researching this field for around thirty years. Their previous work investigated cancer cases caused by infections in 1990, 2002, 2008, 2012, and 2018.

The proportion of cancer cases caused by infections may appear to have dropped during those years (from a high of 18% in 2002), but the authors stress these comparisons cannot really be made confidently, as the sources and quality of the data have changed over time.

item.title: ‘Before I Forget’: A touching and surprisingly funny memoir on caring for ageing abusive parents
item.description: In writing about trauma, French writer Anne Pauly is also acerbically funny and no one is spared from her arch humour.
item.content:encoded:
How do you mourn an abusive alcoholic parent? French writer Anne Pauly’s Before I Forget, translated by Dina Leifer, addresses this question in a deeply personal account of grief.

We accompany Pauly’s protagonist and narrator, Anne, as she cares for her ailing father, looking after his house and his personal grooming. Having grown up witnessing her father’s recurrent violence towards her mother, Pauly addresses some very serious topics. She expresses anger towards people who cannot understand why victims of domestic abuse don’t simply leave, saying:

“I’d like to see you, on a Sunday evening, your eye black and blue and your nightshirt torn, hurriedly pack a case for a strip-lit emergency refuge. I’d like to see you, bombarded by insults and threats, find the energy to run to the station with your children and get on a train, not knowing whether you can ever come back.”

In the present, this giant who would chase Anne’s mother around the kitchen table or lock his family out of their home in a drunken rage has been reduced to a sunken form in a wheelchair. These two versions of him co-exist in the narrative.

item.title: Maharashtra’s recognition of women farmers will break gender barriers
item.description: Women Farmers Certificates will recognise women engaged in agriculture or allied activities as farmers, even when they do not own the land.
item.content:encoded:
On October 2, Maharashtra is set to begin issuing the Women Farmers Certificates under the newly enacted Women Farmer’s Empowerment Act 2026. The certificates will formally recognise women engaged in agriculture or allied activities as farmers, even when they do not own the land.

The Women Farmers Certificates will open doors for lakhs of women who sow, tend, harvest and manage our agri-foods systems, as well as livestock, poultry and fisheries, but are often left out of the formal definition of a farmer. Maharashtra has shown political will and a clear sense of urgency in bringing women farmers’ needs into the spotlight and leading by example.

Feminisation of agriculture

We have been witnessing feminisation of agriculture for some time now. As men move to non-farm jobs, women have increasingly taken up the role of managing and maintaining the agricultural lands.

But this has often meant more responsibility without a corresponding rise in control, assets or decision-making power. Without land titles, they also struggle to access critical resources such as credit, water, technology and extension services, reducing them to labourers in a sector they largely sustain.

item.description: Published in 1988, Deshpande’s book received the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1990.

“I had often found family life unendurable. Worse than anything else had been the boredom of the unchanging pattern, the unending monotony. I remember now how often I had sighed for a catastrophe, a disaster, no, not a personal one, but anything to shake us out of our dull grooves.”

Jaya, in Shashi Deshpande’s 1988 novel That Long Silence, is a rare Indian housewife – she hates the dullness of “family life” and the utter boredom of domestic chores. Being needed by her family does not make her proud; in fact, she resents being seen as just the wife and the mother, forever at the beck and call of her moody husband and children.

item.title: ‘Beyond Our Births’: A debut novel questions the validity of a person’s identity markers
item.description: Antara Mukherjee’s novel is a meditation on love – of its undefined, inexplicable nature, and its borderless provenance.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond Our Births, Antara Mukherjee’s debut novel, is an exploration of the location of identity. Its narrative – that of a child abandoned by her Bangladeshi Muslim parents, adopted by a West Bengali Hindu family, forced to leave when the family’s fortunes turn, accompanied back to Bangladesh by her parents, only to escape from them soon after – continually questions the validity of our identity markers: caste, class, religion, nationality, gender; and underlines their intersectionality in our daily lives.

But the novel is perhaps even more a meditation on love – of its undefined, inexplicable nature, and its borderless provenance: for neither bloodlines nor boundaries between nations, or that between the human and animal can contain it. Nimki, the protagonist of the novel, whom we see grow from five to 15, feels the greatest kinship with Bagha – the family dog of the Senguptas, with whom she lives in Kolkata. “Their lack of language”, we are told, “made them understand each other. They could neither hurt nor delve deep, but heal each other nevertheless with their faithful empathy.”

Nimki needed this empathy as compensation for her perpetual hunger for love in a household that gave her shelter but couldn’t instil a sense of belonging....

item.title: How Modi put Delhi under siege to protect Gyanesh Kumar
item.description: Barricades, tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel as well as right-wing goons were deployed to stop the protests against vote rigging.
item.content:encoded:
What does authoritarianism sound like?

In Delhi’s posh Connaught Place on Saturday, it was the drone of automated police announcements, broadcast on loop from loudspeakers fitted on spiked poles.

“Making groups, taking out marches or any other action is barred,” a robotic voice announced. “Everyone should peacefully move out from here and follow the police’s orders.”

A few feet away, the intersection bristled with paramilitary troops waiting to pounce on any protester they could spot. On the other side was a wall of yellow barricades. The street was empty. The Delhi Police had blocked off almost all traffic to Connaught Place, the city centre.

This unprecedented bandobast was intended to stop demonstration against Gyanesh Kumar, India’s Chief Election Commissioner, who protestors allege has rigged the voter rolls to favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On Saturday, the Modi government pulled out all stops to protect Kumar.

To prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar, a legally designated protest site a few hundred metres from Connaught Place, the Delhi Police cordoned off the city centre with several layers of barricades. item.title: TM Krishna: For generations, ‘Hum Dekhenge’ has stripped the cloak off powerful narcissists
item.description: In Iqbal Bano’s rendition, a song of protest that seeks to unsettle the powerful and foretells their downfall is cased in a delicate, poised melody.
item.content:encoded:
As protesters all over India demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner and the restoration of every citizen’s voting rights, I offer this musical note of solidarity.

For generations, Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s Hum Dekhenge has been an integral part of protests, a metaphor for resistance, justice and democracy, and since 2019 it has seeped into our wider national consciousness. While its history and lyrical depth is well known, the song’s musical cadence is less discussed. The gold standard for this song is without doubt the rendition by Iqbal Bano in her stirring protest against Zia-ul-Haq, and that is the basis of this piece.

Hum Dekhenge is not an activist’s chanting song, shrill in tonality, fast in tempo, with an un-decorative melody. It is simple, yet nuanced in its flow and melodic direction. Iqbal Bano’s rendition is unusually slow, embedded with filigree work and subtle movements that allow the song to unfold evocatively.

The way Bano renders Woh din ke jiskaa vaada hai, with jiskaa meandering ever so slightly, followed by a stunning musical drop at vaada hai leading sharply to hum dekhenge is stunning. She follows that up with a tantalising glide across the octave, sensuously singing the phrase jo lauh-e-azal me likha hai.

item.title: ‘Darkness and Other Stories’: A collection of Razia Sajjad Zaheer’s politically conscious fiction
item.description: This collection, translated from the Urdu by Saba Mahmood Bashir, will appeal to scholars of gender studies, Partition studies, and postcolonial literature.
item.content:encoded:
In the short story “Darkness,” from the collection Darkness and Other Stories – translated from the Urdu by Saba Mahmood Bashir – Razia Sajjad Zaheer describes a train journey whose anxieties are all too familiar to Muslims today. The protagonist is Zaheer herself, who has boarded her train at the Old Delhi Railway Station and is headed for Amritsar.

We are reminded of Rasheed Jahan, another fiery progressive writer, whose “Dilli ki Sair” had chalked out a different struggle – a woman who must idly wait at the Delhi railway station amidst strange men, a stand-by object like the luggage itself, while her husband struts about with an old friend. But Zaheer is not bound to any consort. She is a university graduate, she is a progressive writer of Urdu fiction; she also happens to be a Muslim woman.

item.title: ‘A focus on literature that is part of everyday life’: Onaiza Drabu on editing a Kashmiri anthology

“I wanted to make the case for the fact that literature is everywhere; it is omnipresent.”

That is what Onaiza Drabu aimed to do with The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, the anthology she has edited that illustrates the richness of Kashmiri literature, land, and people through a diverse canon of expressions.

The anthology brings together the works of several historical saints, scholars, unlettered poets, and voices of Kashmir, ranging from the fourteenth century to the contemporary era.

In a conversation with Scroll, Drabu spoke about the making of The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, the inspiration for the project, the process of collecting literary works from earlier centuries and selecting texts for an anthology of this scale.

item.title: How TV channels covered the protests as ‘anarchy’ and ignored the detentions of journalists
item.description: The police allowed mainstream television channels to broadcast from Central Delhi while restricting access for several reporters from independent media.
item.content:encoded:
Around 4.30 pm on Saturday, Republic TV, the news channel helmed by Arnab Goswami, flashed this headline on television screens across the country: “CJP Flop Show”.

It referred to the protests in Delhi, called by the Cockroach Janta Party and Left student outfits, against the special intensive revision of voter lists – a controversial exercise that has disenfranchised millions, driving many Indians to take to the streets and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

By the time Republic TV flashed that headline, credible reports about the police having detained over a dozen journalists for simply reporting on the protests, including three from Scroll, had been in circulation for hours. Many of these journalists were detained while they were documenting how the police were clamping down on protesters.

The high-handedness of the authorities, even towards fellow members of the press, found no mention in Republic TV’s coverage. The same broadly held true for other Hindi and English television news channels as well. Their reporters and anchors limited themselves to broadcasting the police and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s point of view on the protests for most of Saturday.

item.title: The Ghanian scholar who changed how the world hears African music
item.description: Kofi Agawu challenged the idea that African music is something that is ‘felt’ rather than thought about analytically.
item.content:encoded:
Kofi Agawu is regarded as one of the world’s foremost authorities on African music. The Ghanaian scholar, teacher and researcher has changed how the world hears and studies it.

I am a scholar of indigenous African music. I have researched and written extensively on African indigenous knowledge systems and worldviews.

I also know Professor Agawu personally. He has visited my institution, the University of Venda in South Africa. In this article, I pay tribute to his pioneering work in African musicology while taking issue with one finer point in his theories. This, I think, makes for a more useful tribute than unbroken praise.

The invention of African rhythm

Kofi Agawu, who turns 70 on 28 September 2026, was born in Hohoe in Ghana’s Volta region. He is Ewe, which is the dominant group of the region. He finished school at Achimota in Accra, studied in Britain and completed a doctorate at Stanford University in 1982. After many years at Princeton, he now teaches at the City University of New York Graduate Center.

Across six books he has made it very hard to go on saying that African music is something that is “felt” rather than something that is thought about analytically.

item.title: Lessons for the 21st century from Mary Shelley’s 1826 novel ‘The Last Man’
item.description: Set in the late 21st century, the novel is about a lethal contagion spread by human conflict that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.
item.content:encoded:
Even if you have never read it, you know the story of Mary Shelley’s second great work of political science fiction after Frankenstein. The Last Man, published in 1826 but set in the late 21st century, tells the tale of a lethal contagion spread by human conflict and war that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.

With wars and climate catastrophes hitting a world still reeling from 7 million deaths caused by Covid-19, Shelley’s pandemic novel has perhaps never felt so relevant.

And the book’s influence is widespread. The tropes and themes of The Last Man have shaped the genre of postapocalyptic fiction in the two centuries since its release. In Shelley’s Frankenstein and the many stories, films and TV shows it has inspired, the abandoned monster becomes a plague upon his creator.

In The Last Man and the countless books and movies on its themes that followed, a human-made epidemic becomes the mega-monster that threatens the extinction of humanity itself.

Some of the recent television series that explore these themes are The Last of Us, Midnight Mass, and Station Eleven. They follow classic films such as I Am Legend, 28 Days Later, and The Last Man on Earth.

Regardless of how many zombie-invasion or vampire-apocalypse movies you have seen, if you haven’t read The Last Man, I recommend you do. And if you have, perhaps read it again.

On Saturday, as the Delhi Police detained thousands of protestors trying to reach Jantar Mantar, Kirti Lal closely followed the news on social media in faraway Indore in Madhya Pradesh.

He watched videos of how leaders of the student group, Cockroach Janata Party – Abhijeet Dipke, Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka – were detained by the Delhi Police from inside the aircraft that had brought them to the national capital. How protestors were bundled into buses even before they could reach the protest venue and how journalists were taken into custody. How Delhi was placed under a lockdown to stop the students from gathering.

“Citizens are being silenced,” said the 69-year-old Lal.

item.title: Manipur: Nine killed within 24 hours in three districts
item.description: Violence began after a 42-year-old woman was shot near her neck in the Kuki-dominated Chassad village.
item.content:encoded:
Nine persons were killed between Friday and Saturday in Manipur’s Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts, the Hindustan Times reported, quoting unidentified police officials.

At least 14 homes were burnt in Kamjong and the district authorities have imposed prohibitory orders within a 400-metre radius of Chassad police station.

The violence followed the death of a 42-year-old woman, who was killed in the Kuki-dominated Chassad village in Naga-majority Kamjong district, reported PTI. A mother of five, the woman was shot near her neck on Friday night during a gunfight between armed groups and security forces.

The gunfight had started after security forces arrested some village volunteers, reported Hindustan Times.

The term “village volunteers” has been used for armed civilians guarding villages since ethnic clashes broke out in the state between the Kuki and Meitei groups in May 2023.

The women’s death on Friday triggered an exchange of fire between Kuki and Naga armed groups, reported PTI. A 22-year-old man was killed in the clashes and at least 14 homes belonging to members of the Kuki and Naga communities were burnt.

Separately, suspected militants opened fire in the Ningchou village, a Tangkhul Naga settlement near the Myanmar border, in Kamjong, reported PTI.

item.title: ‘Allah Miyan’s Workshop’: Explorations of faith and prejudice in a boy’s coming-of-age story
item.description: Mohsin Khan’s novel has been translated from the Urdu by Maaz Bin Bilal.
item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, I like to pick up a book without reading anything about it first. Sometimes, it is just the blurb, or perhaps only the title. Nothing else. Sometimes, the fact that a translator decided to translate a certain novel is enough. I find it satisfying to let a story tell itself on its own terms. I’m willingly led by it – I do not try to anticipate where it is headed. Urdu writer Mohsin Khan’s novel Allah Miyan’s Workshop, translated by Maaz Bin Bilal, turned out to be one such book for me. I picked it up knowing almost nothing about it, and perhaps that was the best way to read it.

A child’s world

The novel’s central character is Gibran, a curious 14-year-old boy living in Awadh. Along with his coming of age, we also follow him as he comes to terms with religion, family, and the expectations placed upon him by his conservative father, who wants him to work at the local mosque. His carefree childhood is interrupted when his father is arrested on suspicion of terrorism.
